title: The First Six Seals: Horsemen, Martyrs, and the Great Day
summary: The Lamb opens six of the seven seals. The first four release riders on white, red, black, and pale horses, bringing conquest, war, famine, and death. The fifth reveals the souls of martyrs under the altar crying out for justice, and the sixth brings cosmic upheaval, as people of every rank hide from the wrath of the One on the throne and of the Lamb.
story: In chapter 5 the Lamb took the sealed scroll. Now he breaks the seals, and what comes out first is not the end but the kind of world the church lives in: conquest, bloodshed, scarcity, and death, all of them given permission and set within limits. Then the scene turns to those who have died for their faithfulness and to the question every suffering believer asks, how long. The sixth seal answers with a glimpse of the final day of reckoning. The chapter ends on a question, “who is able to withstand it?”, and chapter 7 will answer it before the seventh seal is opened.
historical:
The first hearers knew all four horsemen from experience. The Parthian empire beyond the Euphrates was Rome's great rival in the east, famous for its mounted archers, and it had humiliated Roman armies at Carrhae in 53 BC and again in AD 62, when a Roman force surrendered at Rhandeia. A crowned rider with a bow may well have made Asian readers think of that threat. The red horse's taking of peace from the earth struck at Rome's proudest boast, the Pax Romana (Roman peace), and the civil wars of AD 68 to 69, when four emperors ruled in a single year, showed how fragile that peace was. Famine and food shortages recur in the period; Acts 11:28 mentions a severe famine under Claudius. Earthquakes were a feature of life in Asia: Tacitus records a quake in AD 17 that ruined twelve cities, including Sardis and Philadelphia, and another that destroyed Laodicea around AD 60.

The price in verse 6 is steep. A denarius was roughly a laborer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2), and a quart of wheat was about one person's daily ration, so a day's work buys bread for one and nothing more. Barley was the cheaper grain of the poor. Why oil and wine are spared is uncertain. Some point out that grain crops fail in drought more quickly than deep-rooted olive trees and vines; others connect the line with an edict of Domitian around AD 92, reported by Suetonius, ordering vineyards in the provinces cut back and then withdrawn.
cultural:
The colored horses come from Zechariah 1 and 6, where horses of different colors patrol the earth for the LORD. The combined judgments of sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts are the four sore judgments of Ezekiel 14:21. The pale horse is literally greenish-pale (Greek chlōros), the color of a corpse; its rider is Death, and Hades (the Greek name for the realm of the dead, used for the Hebrew Sheol) follows him.

The souls under the altar draw on sacrificial practice. In the tabernacle the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7), and the martyrs' lives have been poured out the same way. Their cry, how long, is the cry of the lament psalms (Psalm 79:5-10) and of the angel in Zechariah 1:12. The white robes they receive signal vindication and purity. The sixth seal gathers the prophets' images for the day of the LORD: the darkened sun and blood-red moon of Joel 2:31, the sky rolled up like a scroll in Isaiah 34:4, and people hiding in the rocks from God's majesty in Isaiah 2:19. The plea to the mountains to fall on them comes from Hosea 10:8, and Jesus used it on the road to the cross (Luke 23:30).
literary: The four horsemen form a tight unit: each seal is opened by the Lamb, each living creature says “Come!”, and each rider is given something, a crown, permission, a sword, authority. That repeated word given marks every power as permitted and limited, never independent. The sequence closely follows Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives in Mark 13, Matthew 24, and Luke 21: wars, conflict among nations, famines, earthquakes, persecution of believers, and then signs in sun, moon, and stars. The fifth seal shifts from earth to the altar in heaven, and the sixth shifts to the whole cosmos. The list in verse 15 moves down the social order from kings to slaves, so no rank escapes. The pattern of six in one movement followed by an interlude before the seventh will repeat with the trumpets (chapters 8 to 11).

outline.t: First seal: the white horse and the conqueror
Second seal: the red horse and war
Third seal: the black horse and famine
Fourth seal: the pale horse, Death and Hades
Fifth seal: the martyrs under the altar
Sixth seal: the great day of wrath

doctrines.note: Every horseman is given his power, and death is limited to a fourth of the earth. The evils of history are real and terrible, but they are not outside God's rule, and they do not have the last word.

The martyrs are told to rest a little longer. Scripture does not explain away the suffering of the faithful, but it places it before God, answers the cry with vindication, and promises that it has an end.

The sixth seal pictures the day when every human power, from kings to slaves, stands before God. The wrath is called the wrath of the Lamb, a deliberate paradox: the one who was slain is also the judge.

words.note: Sphragis, seal. A seal of wax or clay closed a document and guaranteed it. Breaking the seals is the Lamb's act of setting God's purposes in motion. In chapter 7 the same word is used for the seal of the living God that marks his servants.

Ekdikeō, to avenge or to vindicate, to give justice to someone who has been wronged. The martyrs are not asking to take revenge but asking God, “holy and true”, to judge. Paul uses the same word group when he tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God (Romans 12:19).

Orgē, wrath. In Scripture God's wrath is not a loss of temper but his settled, just opposition to evil. The phrase “the wrath of the Lamb” is startling on purpose: the one who died for sinners is not indifferent to evil.

Marturia, testimony or witness. The martyrs died for the word of God and the testimony they held. From this word group the English word martyr comes, since in the early church witness so often cost a life.

christ: The Lamb opens every seal. Whatever the four horsemen represent, they ride out only when he breaks the seal, which means the suffering of history is under the authority of the one who himself suffered. The martyrs belong to him: they die for the testimony, as he did, and their blood is poured out like a sacrifice, as his was. And the chapter ends by naming him as judge, in the startling phrase the wrath of the Lamb. The one who entered the world as a slaughtered lamb is the same one before whom the powerful will one day stand. Jesus himself spoke of the same sequence of wars, famines, earthquakes, and persecution as the beginning of birth pains, not the end (Mark 13:7-8).

hard.q: The martyrs ask God to avenge their blood. Isn't that at odds with Jesus' command to love enemies?
hard.a:
It can sound like a prayer for revenge, and readers are right to notice it. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did the same as he died (Acts 7:60).

Several things are worth weighing. First, the martyrs do not take vengeance; they entrust it to God, which is exactly what the New Testament asks of believers (Romans 12:19). Second, their cry is the cry of the lament psalms, which Scripture preserves as faithful prayer, not as sin to be edited out. Third, the request is for justice to be done in public, for God to show that the world's verdict on them was false; a God who never judged would leave murderers vindicated and victims forgotten. Many interpreters also note that Revelation keeps the door of repentance open even in judgment (9:20-21; 11:13; 14:6-7). Readers differ on how to hold love of enemies and longing for justice together, but the Bible holds both, and so do these martyrs, who are told to rest and wait rather than to strike.

questions: Each horseman is given his power and a limit. How does it help or trouble you to think of suffering as permitted but bounded?
The martyrs pray “How long?” Have you ever prayed like that, and what did you need from God when you did?
In verse 15 kings and slaves alike hide from God. What do people hide behind today when they feel exposed before him?
